summary_md: Rammstedt and colleagues document how the 15-item BFI-2-XS (and the 30-item BFI-2-S where fielded) was translated into 39 versions for 29 countries in 24 languages for the PIAAC 2023 social-emotional skills module. The procedure is a modified TRAPD: reuse and review of pre-existing translations for 15 languages, double translation plus reconciliation for nine languages (12 versions), national and expert review, independent linguistic verification, and Field Trial pretesting on nearly 30,000 respondents. Change requests were coded into a customized MQM error typology. Before the Field Trial, gendering drove 49 percent of requests and, on average, 10 percent of BFI-2-S items changed per version (range 0 to 80 percent). After it, 13 of 39 versions changed, averaging 6 percent of XS items. The paper is instrument documentation. It reports no reliability, factor structure or invariance results, because Field Trial data are confidential, and the authors say the versions are not yet fully validated. Their comparability claim rests on the procedure, not on data. For Paul's systems the bearing is thin. Melange reads Big Five traits from English political text with closed-vocabulary rates and a 20-item IPIP-style LLM rater, not with self-report questionnaires, and it does no translation. Two transferable lessons follow. First, small wording changes are treated as material to comparability, which matches the itemset versioning the LLM reader already does. Second, comparability across administrations is asserted procedurally rather than shown, which is the gap the system itself hit when interview-derived affective N failed to transfer to floor and hearing text. The paper offers no validity evidence that the system could borrow.

bearings.paper_claim: Item rewording is treated as a comparability risk: each change request was coded by MQM type and approved only for major issues, 3 requests were rejected as preferential, and mean item change was 10 percent per version pre-Field-Trial (range 0-80) and 6 percent post (range 0-53, 13 of 39 versions).
bearings.paper_location: Review of the Initial Versions pp.16-17; Review of the Tested Versions pp.17-18; Figure 2
bearings.system_side: The LLM reader uses 20 IPIP-style observer-keyed items (4 per trait), not BFI-2 items. Any change to item text or keying is a new itemset version and a new cache key. v2 rewrote C1, C2, C4, E4 and S2 after ceiling effects of 86-94 percent on 202 pilot chunks.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only as a governance analogy. Translation of self-report items is a different measurement problem from an LLM rater applying observer items to political text. The paper reports no psychometric consequences of its changes, so it cannot calibrate how much rewording matters. The system's itemset versioning already enforces the point.

bearings.paper_claim: The authors argue that a standardized, parallel adaptation makes the 39 versions more likely to be comparable than independent national translations. They report no psychometric evidence for this: multi-group CFA alignment was run on Field Trial data (about 450 to 1,800 respondents per country) but the results are confidential, and the versions are described as not yet fully validated.
bearings.paper_location: Discussion p.19; Aims p.3; fn.3 p.14
bearings.system_side: Every lexical trait z is standardized within the current speech corpus, so scores are comparable only inside that corpus. Genre transfer of interview-derived affective N to floor and hearing text failed (rho .050 and .161), per the component record.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The analogy maps languages and countries onto speech genres (interview, floor, hearing, social). It supports demanding empirical invariance evidence before pooling or comparing scores across genres, rather than relying on a uniform procedure. It provides no method or numbers the system could import.

gaps_exposed: The system never assesses formal measurement invariance (multi-group CFA or alignment) of its text-derived traits across speech genres or party groups. It relies on within-corpus z-scores and on one-off genre-transfer checks.

The LLM reader's item battery is IPIP-style and written for the project. It has no external item-level validation of the kind that established inventories such as BFI-2 have, and this paper would not supply any.
flags: The item metadata tag measurement-invariance overstates the paper. It reports no invariance results, only that alignment analyses were run centrally on confidential data.
There is an internal inconsistency on language count: p.2 says 23 languages, while the abstract and p.15 say 24.
Editorial conflict: the first author is Editor-in-Chief of the publishing journal, and two co-authors are Associate Editors (p.20).
None of the brain rules are triggered. The paper makes no SNA, LDA, reciprocity or influence claims.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotated-bibliography entry and no markup for this work (paul_entries empty, 0 annotations), so there is no takeaway to check or to find stale. His recorded positions on the psychometrics components cite Ramey and Birkenmaier and Lechner. This paper neither supports nor contradicts them, because it concerns cross-language self-report questionnaires, not text-based trait inference.

related.why: This paper is the source of the BFI-2 hierarchical inventory, from which the BFI-2-S and BFI-2-XS forms translated here are drawn. Soto is a co-author of both.
This meta-analysis gives the LIWC-to-Big-Five correlations that bear on Melange's text-derived traits, which is the validity side that Rammstedt's documentation paper omits.
It is another Big Five self-report work in the vault. It concerns trait-behaviour links under pressure, the mechanism the affective-N slot cites, while Rammstedt concerns instrument comparability.
